assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 120 agent runs/s at peak: 55% new runs, 35% status polls from the UI, 8% resumed runs, 2% async tool callbacks.

assumptions.subject: architecture
assumptions.statement: FAN-OUT IS MODELLED AS REPEATED SERIAL VISITS. A run makes 3 model calls (plan, then one per specialist subtask) and dispatches 2 subtasks, written as repeated steps on the run path. The arrival rates this produces are exact; the LATENCY IS AN UPPER BOUND, because the v1 engine sums service time along a path and has no parallel-fan-out primitive. Real parallel subtasks finish closer to max(subtask) than to their sum.

assumptions.subject: llm
assumptions.statement: The hosted model provider is modelled as the model API gateway in front of it (v1 has no per-instance price for an external API, so giving the provider its own priced node would invent a number). Capacity is the provisioned provider quota: 4 pools x 4,000 requests/minute, about 268 model calls/s. This is the design's binding constraint - the servers have headroom the provider quota does not.

assumptions.subject: llm
assumptions.statement: 7,000 input and 800 output tokens per agent model call; tool schemas plus accumulated conversation state dominate the prompt. Monthly volume = peak call rate / 4 x 2,592,000 s.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: Prompt caching is NOT modelled (the engine has no cache-read token rate), and agent prompts are exactly the case where a cached tool-schema prefix saves the most. The token line is an upper bound.

assumptions.subject: worker
assumptions.statement: 40 subtasks/s per worker instance: a tool-using subtask is I/O bound at roughly 3 s with about 120 concurrent slots.

assumptions.subject: state
assumptions.statement: Run state is written once per run and once per resume; status polls read the cache and fall through to the state store 15% of the time.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: Egress is billed per response: ~12 KB per completed run, ~1 KB per status poll, ~256 B per tool callback.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: The model gateway carries NO compute and NO per-request charge: v1 has no per-instance price for this kind, and a self-hosted proxy has no per-request SKU, so inventing either would be worse than the gap. Its whole cost line is the provider token spend.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The write primary is a SINGLE instance and the engine reports it as a single point of failure. That is the shape of the design: high availability comes from Multi-AZ standby failover, which v1 cannot express - `instances` means active capacity, and a warm standby serves no traffic. Budget for it (the RDS price band tops out at Multi-AZ) and treat the SPOF flag as a reminder, not a modelling error.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Latency here is an UPPER BOUND. The engine queues each component as a single server (M/M/1 sojourn), so a component with a multi-second service time running hot shows a large waiting term. A provider quota is really hundreds of concurrent slots, which queues far better than one server; read the model-call latency as pessimistic and the ARRIVAL and UTILISATION figures as the trustworthy part.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Retries, guardrail rejections and loop-until-done iterations are NOT modelled: v1 has no feedback edge, so a run that re-plans three times appears as one run. Real model-call volume is higher than shown.

_library.summary: A supervisor agent that plans, fans work out to specialist workers over a queue, and resumes from durable run state.
